A privilege to contribute to a country that my family and I are proud to call home.

Today, I signed the pledge reaffirming loyalty to the United Arab Emirates and to the vision of His Highness Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.

For me, this moment is particularly meaningful.

After spending much of my career across Europe and the United States, and nearly two decades in London, my husband and I made the decision to move our family to Abu Dhabi in 2024. It was not a move we had to make, it was a move we wanted to make.

We chose the UAE because of the values we saw here: safety, ambition, openness, respect, and a belief that people from all backgrounds can contribute to something bigger than themselves.

As parents of three children, we wanted them to grow up in an environment that is truly international, where diversity is lived every day, where opportunities are abundant, and where they can learn resilience, curiosity, and respect for different cultures.

Professionally, I have dedicated my career to helping leaders, teams, and organizations unlock their potential through leadership, culture, employee experience, and coaching. Since arriving in Abu Dhabi, I have had the privilege of working with leaders across sectors who are shaping the future of their organizations and contributing to the remarkable transformation taking place across the region.

What continues to inspire me is the UAE’s ability to think long-term while never losing sight of people. The vision, optimism, and commitment to building a better future are visible everywhere, from education and innovation to community and public service.

This pledge is more than a symbolic gesture. For me, it represents a commitment to give back to a country that has welcomed us so warmly, to contribute through my work, to support the development of leaders, to build bridges across cultures, and to help create environments where people can thrive.

Thank you, UAE, for the opportunities, the trust, and the inspiration.

One of my recent reads from Harvard Business Review reinforced something I see repeatedly in executive coaching:

Leadership hiring is not a recruitment decision. It’s a business decision.

Too often, organisations focus on experience and technical expertise, yet many leadership transitions fail because there is a mismatch between the leader and the context they are stepping into.

A leader can be highly successful in one environment and struggle in another. Context matters.

The most successful transitions are not won during the interview process. They are won in the first few months, when leaders must build trust, understand the culture, navigate stakeholders, and establish credibility.

Before making any leadership appointment, I believe organisations should ask:

👉 What does success look like in this specific context?

👉 What behaviours and mindset will be required to achieve it?

Because leadership transitions are not just role changes, they are identity shifts.

When you think about the best leaders you’ve worked with, what did they do in their first few months that set them apart?


#LeadershipDevelopment #ExecutiveCoaching #LeadershipTransitions #SuccessionPlanning #TalentManagement

By the Grace of Almighty Allah I am starting a weekly series  Emotional Intelligence with Work Scenarios, Insights and Reflection as the concept is known but refresher with scenarios will further enhance the understanding but still it requires practice 
Note : Masood is an imaginary Character in these Discussions 
  
 🎯 THE GAP BETWEEN WHO WE ARE AND WHO THEY SEE
 Most of us think we are good listeners. often, we are not
  
 1. ⁉️REFLECTION QUESTIONS TO ASK
• ❓When did I last actively seek feedback on how I come across, not just on what I deliver?
• ❓What's one thing I believe about myself that I have never actually verified?
• ❓What's the smallest, specific change I could commit in me this week
  
2. 👨‍💼 WORKPLACE SCENARIO
  At a leadership off site years into his career, Masood received his first real 360-degree feedback report.  He had always believed he was an exceptional listener  it was part of how he saw himself as a leader, something he thought  would have in hum  if asked to name one of his strength. His direct reports rated him well below where he rated himself, on exactly that competency. He was genuinely stunned. Nobody had ever told him directly, and he had never actually asked.
  
3. 💎 THE INSIGHT
💎Emotional intelligence is not a score, and it cannot be improved by reading about it. Below 3 questions do more work than any framework Masood has coached with since,  
First: How does Our Own self-perception differ from our reputation? 
Second: What matters to Us, genuinely, not what we think should matter? 
Third: What specific behavior will We change, this week, not eventually?
Skip the first and we can guess only. 
Skip the second and we won't sustain the change once it gets uncomfortable. 
Skip the third and it stays a nice conversation for us with no consequence or outcome for enhancement as a Leader. 
💎The uncomfortable research finding behind all of this. Only a little over one third of people can accurately identify their own emotions as they happen which means most of us are navigating our reactions, and our reputations, half-blind and an important Area which Leaders really struggle. Narrowing the Gap of Who we feel and Who they think is a Continuous Transformation in Leadership.
💎Self Awareness check by resonance, feedback, listening and pulse of the room is what Leaders Really Miss in Leading Teams and Its Not Extra Effort It’s the Real Effort not for Them but for Us.

In a world where everyone calls themselves a coach, I decided to take a different path.

One that takes a year of coaching school and mentorship, hundreds of hours of practice, rigorous ethics training, and passing a globally recognised credentialing exam to complete.

Not because a certificate makes you a good coach.

But because that journey gives you something far more valuable than a title — a deep understanding of what coaching actually is.

And more importantly, what it is NOT.

Coaching is not advice.
It is not therapy.
It is not mentoring.
It is not telling you what to do.

It is a rigorous, ethical, client-centred process that creates the conditions for YOU to find your own answers, make your own choices, and move forward on your own terms.

Today I am proud to share that I have earned my ICF Associate Certified Coach (ACC) credential — a globally recognised standard of professional coaching excellence.

A huge thank you to Coaching.LT and Povilas Petrauskas MCC, ACTC for building a program that goes far beyond technique — one that challenges you to truly understand the philosophy, ethics, and depth of what real coaching means. I wouldn't be here without it.

And thank you to the International International Coaching Federation Federation for setting and upholding the global standard that makes this credential mean something.

If you've ever wondered what real coaching looks like, I'd love to show you.

Not every session belongs on a Zoom call.

A client reached out recently. She needed to talk — not just to think things through, but to feel supported while doing it. We could have scheduled an online call. That's the default. It's efficient, convenient, and works most of the time.

But this time was different.

She needed presence. The kind that no AI tool, no video call, no voice note can replicate. The kind that comes from someone physically being in the room with you.

So I showed up.

Because coaching isn't just about the framework or the questions or the process. It's about the relationship. And relationships aren't built only on contracts and structured sessions. Sometimes they're built on the moments when you simply show up for someone.

In a world moving fast toward automation and efficiency, I think we're at risk of forgetting that human presence is still irreplaceable.

Sometimes the most powerful thing you can offer is just being there.

The ones who outperform think about it in terms of positioning.

I’ve seen this play out repeatedly across projects in Dubai. Two identical apartments in the same building. One renovated to “look nice.” One renovated with a clear answer to: who is this for, and what do they expect to pay?

The second one doesn’t just rent faster.

It competes in a different market entirely.

The right finishes don’t just improve aesthetics — they determine your tenant profile, your achievable rent, and your yield. That’s not a design decision. That’s a strategic one.

Renovation isn’t a cost centre.

It’s a positioning decision.

If you own a property in Dubai and haven’t thought about it this way — that’s usually where the upside is hiding.

After months of writing and reflecting, I'm excited and a little emotional to share that my first book, Make Life Click, is now on Amazon Kindle.
It started with an uncomfortable realisation. When you study human behaviour deeply enough, you don't just observe other people. You become your own first subject. 

So I did. I looked at my own patterns and changed what needed changing. The cobbler's children have no shoes, but in my case I had actually made a pair. The hard part wasn't making them. It was learning to keep them on. 
That is what Make Life Click is about. 

The premise is simple. Most people are living one of three lives: the one they inherited, the one they perform, or the one they designed. This book is about the third, and how to keep living it. The aim is for you to become your own coach. 

So I'm curious. Which one are you living right now? Tell me in the comments. I read every response. 

The Amazon link is in the first comment. And if someone came to mind as you read this, please pass it on. They are exactly who I wrote it for.

When you catch yourself in Room 2, what usually brings you back to Room 1?

Is your current leadership style sustainable for the next 24 months, or are you running on corporate adrenaline?

When an enterprise scales, executive teams often mistake task saturation and constant firefighting for operational momentum. They wear 70-hour workweeks like a badge of honor, relying on caffeine, relentless pressure, and sheer force of will to hit their targets.

But running an executive suite on corporate adrenaline is an expensive, short-term strategy. Eventually, the adrenaline wears off. Decisions slow down, strategic clarity degrades into reactive triage, and your top growth drivers hit a wall—leaving your scaling timeline exposed to sudden leadership fatigue and unexpected turnover.

This is why high-altitude executive coaching is an operational necessity.
Coaching isn't an extended therapy session or a temporary wellness perk. It is a clinical mirror that targets the root operational and psychological blocks. It helps leaders:

- Audit Systemic Friction: Identify and eliminate self-imposed operational bottlenecks and micromanagement traps.

- Reclaim Strategic Agency: Shift focus away from daily tactical noise back to 24-month horizon planning.

- Build Sustainable Execution: Replace high-stress adrenaline loops with repeatable, high-leverage decision architectures.

High-velocity growth requires stamina, not sacrifice.

#TalentPrecision #ExecutiveCoaching #LeadershipSustainability #NextGearHR

What Is Career Coaching? A Practical Guide for Professionals
Learn what career coaching is, how sessions work, who benefits, and how to decide whether a career coach is right for your next professional step.
By Yousef Salimah, ICF ACC
17 July 2026
8 min read
Quick answer
Career coaching is a structured, confidential partnership that helps you clarify professional goals, understand what is shaping your choices, evaluate options, and take accountable action. A coach does not choose for you or simply give advice; the process helps you make stronger decisions for yourself.
Career decisions are rarely difficult because people have no options. They are difficult because several priorities compete at the same time: security, growth, meaning, income, family commitments, identity, and fear of making the wrong move. Career coaching creates a disciplined space to work through that complexity.

Reflect.

The questions every leader should ask before September.

There is something special about returning home. Spending time in Cyprus and watching the sea reminded me that some of our best leadership insights come not from doing more, but from creating space to pause, reflect and reset before September begins.

For many leaders, August offers something that the rest of the year rarely does: space.

Space to think.
Space to recharge.
Space to step back from the daily demands of leadership.

Before you switch off for your summer break, take a few moments to reflect.

Ask yourself:

• What am I most proud of so far this year?
• What leadership habit do I want to leave behind?
• Which conversation have I been postponing?
• Where does my team need more from me when we return?
• What do I want to be known for by the end of the year?
• If September were a fresh start, what would I do differently from day one?

The strongest leaders don't just use holidays to rest.

They use them to reset.

Sometimes, the most valuable preparation for September isn't a new plan—it's a better perspective.

Which of these questions will you take with you into your summer break

I've watched capable leaders step into bigger roles and fail to deliver. Not one of them was short on technical skill.

The most expensive line in a value-creation plan is not the capex. It's the senior hire who could not carry the team.

At that level, everyone on the shortlist has the hard skills. What decides delivery is 𝗲𝗺𝗼𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 — the softest-sounding item on any scorecard, and the thing that most often explains a wrong hire.

And it rarely announces itself as a failure. It shows up in 𝗺𝗶𝗰𝗿𝗼-𝗺𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀: 
↳ The leader with the right answer, but not the conviction to hold it in the room.
↳ The outburst in a meeting that costs months of trust.
↳ The blind spot everyone can see except the person standing in it.
↳ Sympathy offered where empathy was needed.
↳ The honest conversation always postponed to next quarter.

None of these show up in an appraisal. All of them show up in the results.

This is the work I do with CXOs and portfolio leadership teams across 10+ countries — performance-linked coaching that builds emotional intelligence alongside the business outcome, not instead of it.

Unlike raw intellect, EI is learnable — at any age, at any level. That's the premise my model rests on: nine soft skills.

🎯Three looking inward — self-perception, self-expression, assertiveness.
🎯Three looking outward — empathy, interpersonal relationships, team performance.
🎯Three under pressure — decision making, problem solving, stress management.

I think of them as bearings on a compass — it never tells you where to go, only where you are pointing.

Of the nine EI soft skills on the compass, which one do you see derail senior people most often? 👇

observations.text:
I have always seen a trap in 0-to-1 launches. Scale-up and value creation get treated as the same thing — and they aren't. Everyone is doing their best — and yet everyone is measuring a different thing.

So I run scale-ups against four scorecards, not one. 

𝗖𝟭 · 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘂𝗺𝗲𝗿 — 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗿𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗯𝗲𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁?
 ↳ Awareness — top-of-mind and spontaneous, tracked quarterly vs competition.
 ↳ Penetration — the most important measure for growth. #HowBrandsGrow
 ↳ Repeat rate — a bigger priority than measuring trials.
 ↳ Clarity Index — how sharply the brand lands the positioning you intended.

𝗖𝟮 · 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗲𝘁𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 — 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘄𝗶𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁?
 ↳ Market share — by geography, by channel, in value and volume.
 ↳ Distribution — numeric in the first quarter, weighted subsequently.
 ↳ Velocity — rate of sale per outlet at a fixed interval, usually monthly.
 ↳ Pricing index — within the defined category and vs the hero competitor.

𝗖𝟯 · 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 — 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗣&𝗟 𝗮𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗲?
 ↳ Gross revenue — in value and volume.
 ↳ Marginal contribution — measured against the pre-launch business case.
 ↳ A&P — marketing and promotion spend, absolute and as a ratio.
 ↳ EBITDA — fixed at business-case stage.

𝗖𝟰 · 𝗖𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 — 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗿𝗴𝗮𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗿𝘆 𝗶𝘁?
 ↳ Alignment — Board, CEO, CMO and Sales Head, all working to one 
    definition of success.
 ↳ Change management — an agile mindset for learning fast and rebounding 
    quickly.
 ↳ Cross-functional working — seamless and without silos, ideally led by the 
    brand team.
 ↳ Nurturing mindset — giving the team space for autonomy and decision-
    making.

The first three Cs get audited. The fourth is what decides whether the other three hold.

If you've led or sponsored a major 0-to-1 scale-up — which “𝗖” resonates best with you? Keen to know your thoughts 👇

I joined RG Brands in Almaty, Kazakhstan for twelve months. I stayed twenty-one. Here's what changed my mind — and three things I'd tell anyone considering career transitions from MNCs to Family-owned businesses. 

In that time the team took two beverage brands, AVA Lemonade and Salam Premium Cola, from a blank page to shelves across Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan. Thank you Hans Dewaele my board sponsor, Timur Kaltayev CEO RG Brands and Natalia Turunkhayeva, my 5-star Senior Brand Manager and the team in RG Brands for your support in my journey🙏

𝐓𝐡𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐈 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐭 𝐦𝐨𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 25 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐠𝐥𝐨𝐛𝐚𝐥 𝐌𝐍𝐂𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝐚 𝐟𝐚𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐲-𝐨𝐰𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐠𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐛𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬:

𝟭. 𝗔𝗰𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗵𝗶𝗱𝗲. In a large MNC a decision can be spread across enough people that nobody quite owns it. Here it stops with you, visibly. Uncomfortable for about a week — then liberating. You spend your time finding the answer instead of reporting on the search for it.

𝟮. 𝗙𝗮𝗺𝗶𝗹𝘆 𝗯𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗮𝘁 𝗮 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗠𝗡𝗖𝘀 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗴𝗼𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗻. Our on-shelf mock-ups and planograms took weeks to build and one meeting to approve. The discipline isn't in the deciding — it's in doing the work beforehand that makes one meeting enough.

𝟯. 𝗧𝗿𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆. Your CV gets you into the room. Your performance earns loyalty. But in a business built on relationships, trust is the ceiling — and it's earned in small unglamorous moments, rarely in the big presentations.

I'm back based between Dubai and Delhi now, doing what I've always done — growing food, beverage and dairy businesses, and coaching the leaders running them. More on that shortly.

If you've made this move — or you're an owner who's brought MNC talent into a family business — I'd love to hear how you made it work. 👇

A leader said something to me in a session recently that I haven't stopped thinking about.

She was talking about playing small. Not trusting her instincts. 𝗛𝗼𝗹𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗶𝗻 𝗿𝗼𝗼𝗺𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘀𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝗮𝗱 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝘂𝗽 𝘀𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗲.

And then she said this:

'𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳, 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘀𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘄𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗴𝗼.'

I didn't say that. She did.

And I think it's one of the truest things I've heard about what actually moves a leader forward.

Because we talk so much about confidence. Presence. Executive gravitas. As if it's something you manufacture or perform.

𝘽𝙪𝙩 𝙨𝙝𝙚 𝙬𝙖𝙨 𝙥𝙤𝙞𝙣𝙩𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙖𝙩 𝙨𝙤𝙢𝙚𝙩𝙝𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙦𝙪𝙞𝙚𝙩𝙚𝙧.

That the move from playing small to showing up fully isn't a push. It's a softening.

You can't get to the next version of yourself while you're still clenched around the frustration of the current one.

𝙏𝙝𝙚 𝙘𝙤𝙢𝙥𝙖𝙨𝙨𝙞𝙤𝙣 𝙘𝙧𝙚𝙖𝙩𝙚𝙨 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙨𝙥𝙖𝙘𝙚. 
𝙏𝙝𝙚 𝙨𝙥𝙖𝙘𝙚 𝙘𝙧𝙚𝙖𝙩𝙚𝙨 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙢𝙤𝙫𝙚𝙢𝙚𝙣𝙩.

I find this work quietly extraordinary. When a leader finds their own language for their own truth — before I've even offered a frame — that's when I know something real is happening.

But as we slowed down and looked at what he actually wanted — really wanted — 𝙨𝙤𝙢𝙚𝙩𝙝𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙨𝙝𝙞𝙛𝙩𝙚𝙙.

He didn't want to manage his team better.
𝗛𝗲 𝘄𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺.

Their capabilities. Their ability to take on complexity without needing him to be the answer every time.

𝙏𝙝𝙖𝙩'𝙨 𝙖 𝙘𝙤𝙢𝙥𝙡𝙚𝙩𝙚𝙡𝙮 𝙙𝙞𝙛𝙛𝙚𝙧𝙚𝙣𝙩 𝙜𝙤𝙖𝙡.

Managing keeps you at the centre.
Developing moves the centre to them.

And when we named that distinction, something visibly landed for him.

Because he'd been trying to solve a team management problem when what he was actually 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗿𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝗮 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝗺𝗯𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.

I keep seeing this with senior leaders. The goal they walk in with is real. It's just rarely the whole truth.

The real goal is usually bigger. And scarier. And much more worth working on.

We talk a lot about playing small.

How to stop it. 
How to push through it. 
How to override the fear and just show up bigger.

𝙄 𝙩𝙝𝙞𝙣𝙠 𝙬𝙚'𝙧𝙚 𝙨𝙤𝙡𝙫𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙬𝙧𝙤𝙣𝙜 𝙩𝙝𝙞𝙣𝙜.

In my experience, the leaders 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘆 𝘀𝘁𝘂𝗰𝗸 𝗶𝗻 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 small aren't failing to push hard enough.

They're resisting 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗳𝘁 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀.

That space 𝙗𝙚𝙩𝙬𝙚𝙚𝙣 𝙬𝙝𝙚𝙧𝙚 𝙮𝙤𝙪 𝙖𝙧𝙚 𝙖𝙣𝙙 𝙬𝙝𝙚𝙧𝙚 𝙮𝙤𝙪 𝙬𝙖𝙣𝙩 𝙩𝙤 𝙜𝙤 is uncomfortable. It asks you to sit with the frustration, the self-doubt, the not-yet. 

Most leaders I work with have been trained their whole career to move fast through discomfort. 

𝗧𝗼 𝗮𝗰𝘁. 𝗧𝗼 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗱𝗲. 𝗧𝗼 𝘀𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗲.

So they resist the space itself.

And when you resist the space, you stay exactly where you are. Not because you lack courage. Because 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗻𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗹𝗲𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳 𝗮𝗿𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝗽𝗼𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗯𝗹𝗲.

The work isn't pushing through playing small.
It's learning to stop fighting the space long enough to actually move through it.

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗿𝘂𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗽𝗮𝘀𝘁 𝗮 𝘀𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗺𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗯𝗲 𝗮𝘀𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘆 𝗮 𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘁𝗹𝗲 𝗹𝗼𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗿?

I watched 𝘁𝘄𝗼 𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗿𝗲𝗻 𝗳𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 recently.

Full intensity. Both certain they were right. Both explaining their story loudly, repeatedly, with complete conviction.

And then 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺 𝘀𝗮𝗶𝗱 𝘀𝗼𝗿𝗿𝘆.

Just that. Nothing more.
And the other one melted.

I've been thinking about that moment ever since.

Because those two children will grow up one day. 
They might work together. 
They might build something together. 
They might sit across a 𝗯𝗼𝗮𝗿𝗱𝗿𝗼𝗼𝗺 𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗼𝗿 𝗮 𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝘀 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗰𝗲𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁.

And they will have forgotten what they knew at ten years old.
That the story 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗸𝗲𝗲𝗽 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀𝗻'𝘁 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.

It creates more misalignment. More fuel. More distance.

I've seen this in family systems. When forgiveness takes time — not because people don't care, but 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗮𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝗯𝘂𝘀𝘆 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗶𝗿 𝘁𝗿𝘂𝘁𝗵. And every explanation, however valid, adds another layer to the wall.

Here's the part nobody talks about.

We are not speaking about 𝗮𝘀𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗴𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀.
We are speaking 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗴𝗶𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝘁.

And the person who gives it, they are not doing it for the other.

They are doing it for themselves.

The moment you give forgiveness, something shifts in you. The energy that was locked in proving your story, 𝗱𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻, 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 - it softens. You step into calm. And from that calm, you can finally see the relationship clearly again.

Space opens.

A new emotion can emerge. Curiosity. Empathy. 
Something that was completely impossible when you were clenched around being right.

This is 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗴𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝗻 𝗮 𝗳𝗮𝗺𝗶𝗹𝘆 𝗯𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺.

It doesn't erase what happened. 
It doesn't mean the other person was right.

𝗜𝘁 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗵𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗺 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝗰𝗮𝘀𝗲.

And when one person in a family system does that really does it, the energy in the room changes.

It always does.

In the 𝘼𝙇𝙄𝙂𝙉 𝙖𝙥𝙥𝙧𝙤𝙖𝙘𝙝, this is what Leverage means at its deepest level. Not just using strengths but using the one internal resource that changes the entire system. Your own willingness to step into calm first.

𝗙𝗼𝗿𝗴𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗱 𝗻𝗼𝗯𝗼𝗱𝘆 𝘀𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗹𝗼𝘂𝗱 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀.

It might be the one that decides whether the business survives the generation.

So, in your family business, 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝘄𝗮𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗼 𝗴𝗼 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁?

Most leaders wait for proof before they believe.

Extraordinary leaders believe before the proof arrives.

Because circumstances don’t create results - belief does.
Here’s how I apply it:

I hold my vision with more seriousness than I hold circumstances. 

What I haven’t seen yet gets treated as just as real as what’s already in front of me.

In the moments when nothing is visible or when the results haven’t landed yet  — I hold on to the belief.

That’s exactly what certainty is.

Not after the proof. Before it.

A decision about what you believe, held so steady that uncertainty has nowhere to grip.

So if you’re leading through a moment where the results haven’t shown up yet — and you’re starting to wonder if your vision was ever realistic -

That’s not a sign to abandon it.

That’s the exact moment certainty is built.
So strengthen the belief.

observations.text:
Six weeks. Endless learning. A lifetime of impact.

As I complete the Stanford Executive Program (SEP), I leave with far more than a certificate. I leave with a transformed perspective on leadership, and a renewed commitment to lead with greater purpose, curiosity, and courage.

For six incredibly intense weeks, our days started early and ended late. We immersed ourselves in leadership, strategy, corporate governance, organizational behavior, culture, innovation, communication, negotiation, entrepreneurship, finance, geopolitics, the profound impact of Artificial Intelligence on business and society, and more.

Stanford didn’t simply expand my knowledge, it reshaped the way I think.

One lesson stands: leadership isn’t about having the right answers. It’s about asking better questions, embracing diverse perspectives, making sound decisions amid uncertainty, and creating cultures where people and ideas can thrive.

One of the greatest highlights was delivering a TED-style talk at Stanford on Emotional Intelligence, a topic that has been at the heart of my work for many years. Sharing that message with such an extraordinary community reinforced my belief that, while AI is transforming the way we work, it is emotional intelligence, judgment, integrity, and humanity that will define the leaders who shape the future.

The SEP faculty were exceptional. Every lecture challenged assumptions, every case study stretched our thinking, and every discussion offered practical insights that will continue to influence how I lead, contribute in the boardroom, and support organizations through transformation.

Equally valuable was the remarkable cohort I had the privilege of learning alongside. Beyond the classroom, we built friendships through shared experiences that I will never forget: 9 hikes, 3 sailing trips, rafting down the American River, countless dinners and gatherings, and cheering together at FIFA World Cup matches. Those moments reminded me that some of life’s greatest lessons are learned outside the classroom and that meaningful relationships are among a leader’s greatest assets.

To the exceptional Stanford faculty, the outstanding team, and my classmates from around the world, thank you for challenging me, inspiring me, and making this journey unforgettable. You have left a lasting legacy mark on both my professional and personal journey.

As I return home, I do so with fresh ideas, lasting friendships, renewed energy, and an even stronger conviction that the future belongs to leaders who never stop learning, never stop evolving, and never stop investing in people.

Leadership is not about reaching the destination. It is about continuously expanding your perspective, elevating those around you, and having the courage to evolve every step of the way.

observations.text:
July filled my heart.

It gave me time to reconnect with the people, places, and purpose that matter most.

Lebanon gave me quiet mornings. Walking through my village with my mom reminded me that the richest conversations happen one step at a time.

Turkey gave me joy. Watching my teenage daughter and my best friend laugh together reminded me that every relationship grows through shared experiences. My daughters’ questions always amaze me and they were many. 

London gave me inspiration. Watching Hamilton left me reflecting on the kind of legacy every leader chooses to build, one conversation and one decision at a time.

Antigua gave me peace. White beaches, endless sunsets, and moments of stillness reminded me that renewal is one of the greatest investments we can make in ourselves.

July also gave me something I had been longing for.

Time to write.

I made meaningful progress on my book, a project that has lived in my heart for years. Every page brought me closer to sharing what I have witnessed after coaching hundreds of leaders across the world.

Success can exist alongside loneliness.
Achievement can coexist with disconnection.
Leadership becomes transformational when people feel seen, valued, and trusted.

These ideas have shaped my coaching for years, and putting them into words has been one of the most fulfilling parts of my summer.

I return to work today carrying fresh ideas, renewed energy, and even stronger conviction that humanizing leadership creates workplaces where people thrive and performance follows.

Every trip gave me memories.

Every conversation gave me perspective.

Every page gave me purpose.

I’m deeply grateful for July.

What filled your heart this summer?

The most effective way to destroy a position of #power is to spend it protecting itself. Trump declared dominion over Netanyahu's decisions. Within hours, Netanyahu acted unilaterally. Starmer framed every welfare retreat as fiscal responsibility. Each retreat made the next one more inevitable.

I've sat in a version of this myself - not at that scale, but the same internal logic. Using authority to manage my own anxiety rather than to honour the people it was meant to serve. It didn't feel like failure at the time. It felt like survival.

This new piece in "At the Edge of Oneself" looks at this pattern from the outside-in, through Trump, Netanyahu, Starmer, and three leaders who appear to be doing it differently: Carney, Chouinard, and Pope Leo XIV. Then it turns closer to home, as this series does.

Where is the power or influence you hold being aimed right now — outward, toward those in your care, or inward, toward your own security?
